chapter_sentences: [heading]Working Toward the Führer.

[break]IAN KERSHAW. The renewed focus, already seen in the mid-nineteen eighties, on the connected histories of the Soviet Union and Germany, especially during the Stalin and Hitler periods, has become much stronger since the changes in Eastern Europe. The increased attention on the horrors of Stalinism has led to efforts to downplay Nazi cruelty - seen as evil, but not as evil as Stalinism (and by extension, communism in general).

The harsh Stalinist experiment in modernization is used to eliminate any connection between modernization and humanizing, civilizing, liberating, or democratic development. This allows the claim that Hitler's regime was also, and deliberately, a "modernizing dictatorship."

All of this suggests a return, despite many improvements and criticisms of the concept since the nineteen sixties, to basic traditional ideas about "totalitarianism" and to seeing Stalin and Hitler as "totalitarian dictators." It is not wrong to compare the forms of dictatorship in Germany under Hitler and in the Soviet Union under Stalin, even though the subject is unpleasant.
Looking at the nature and extent of their inhumanity is also acceptable. The concept of totalitarianism allows for a comparison of various techniques and tools of domination.

This kind of comparison is valid on its own. The basic idea is that both regimes made total claims on society. These claims were based on a monopoly of certain ideological demands and led to extreme levels of repression, as well as efforts to indoctrinate, manipulate, and mobilize people. This gave these regimes a unique energy that is not found in more traditional authoritarian regimes. This idea also seems mostly uncontested.

However, the main issue with the term "totalitarianism" - ignoring how it is used in non-scholarly contexts - is that it is a descriptive concept, not a theory. It does not explain much. It assumes that Stalinism and Hitlerism were more similar than different. But the basis for this comparison is weak, mostly limited to the structures of governance.

[break]My starting point in these thoughts is the assumption that, even though the two regimes had some similar forms of domination on the surface, they were essentially more different than similar. While I believe there is more value in comparing Nazism with other fascist movements and systems than with the Soviet system, I still want to focus on the unique aspects of the Nazi dictatorship and the need to explain these.

I also want to explain the features that can be seen as common parts of European fascism after the First World War, by looking at the specific dominant elements of German political culture. (Here I admit to a currently unpopular belief in the idea of a special German path, or Sonderweg.) Sometimes, pointing out differences can be more useful than looking at similarities.

Here, I want to use what I understand, based on my limited knowledge of recent historical writing on Stalinism, to be key aspects of Stalin's dictatorship to show some important differences in the Hitler regime. I hope this will help form a basis for thinking about a central question in understanding the Third Reich: what caused the increasing push toward radicalization, the drive toward destruction in the Third Reich?

A lot of the answer, I want to suggest right away, has to do with the breakdown and collapse of what might be called "rational" systems of rule, a system of "ordered" government and administration. But what led to this collapse, and, most importantly, what role did Hitler play in it? These questions are at the heart of my investigation. First, I want to list some key differences between the Stalinist and Hitlerist regimes.

[break][item]Stalin came up through within a system of government, as one of its main supporters. He was, as Roland Suny says, a committee man, top leader, man of the machine; and, in Moshe Lewin's words, 'bureaucracy's anti-Christ', the 'creature of his party', who.

[break]became a despot by controlling the power at the heart of the party, in its secretariat. In a way, it's tempting to draw a comparison in the German situation, looking at Bormann's role rather than Hitler's. Could Stalin have said something like Hitler did in nineteen forty-one: "I've totally lost sight of the Party organizations.

When I find myself facing one or another of these developments, I say to myself: 'By God, how that has grown!'"? Hitler was a party leader and head of government who cared little for bureaucracy and was not the kind of person who worked well in committees or political machines. Before 1933, he had no real involvement in the Nazi Movement's bureaucratic side.

After 1933, when he became head of government, he rarely wrote anything himself, only signing laws that were placed in front of him by Lammers. The Four-Year Plan Memorandum from nineteen thirty-six is the only major policy document from nineteen thirty-three to nineteen forty-five that Hitler wrote himself.

He wrote it in frustration and anger at the position taken during the nineteen thirty-five through thirty-six economic crisis by Schacht and some parts of business and industry. Remarkably, Hitler only gave copies of his memorandum to two people, Göring and Blomberg (later giving a third copy to Speer). The Economics Minister was not even on the short list of people who received it!

Business and industrial leaders were not told that the memorandum existed. Hitler's way of operating was not good for running an orderly government. After the first year or two of the dictatorship, he started acting more and more like the party leader from the nineteen twenties.

His lifestyle was even similar to what his friend Kubizek described about Hitler's lazy habits when he was a young man in Linz and Vienna. One of his former adjutants gave this account after the war: Hitler usually showed up just before lunch. He quickly read through the press cuttings from Reich Press Chief Dietrich and then went to eat.

It became harder and harder for Lammers, the head of the Reich Chancellory, and Meissner, the head of the Presidial Chancellory, to get him to make decisions that only he, as head of state, could make.

When Hitler stayed at Obersalzberg, it was even worse. He never left his room before two p.m. Then he went to lunch. He spent most afternoons walking. In the evening, right after dinner, there were films. He didn't like reading documents. I have sometimes gotten decisions from him, even on important matters, without him ever asking to see the related files.

He believed that many things would sort themselves out if you didn't get involved. As this comment points out, even Lammers, the only link between Hitler and the state ministries (whose leaders had stopped meeting as a cabinet by early nineteen thirty-eight), sometimes had trouble getting to Hitler and getting decisions from him.

For example, Lammers himself wrote a sad letter to Hitler's adjutant on October twenty-first, nineteen thirty-eight, asking for a meeting to report to the Führer on several urgent issues that had piled up since his last detailed report, which was on four September.

[break]Hitler's growing distance from the government bureaucracy and the main parts of the state shows more than just a difference in style compared to Stalin's way of doing things. I think it shows a deeper difference in the nature of the two regimes, as seen in the role of each leader. I will come back to this point later.

[break]Stalin was a dictator who intervened heavily, sending many letters and instructions to shape or interfere with policy. He chaired all key committees. His goal seems to have been taking complete control of all decision-making and concentrating it in the Politburo. He wanted to centralize state power and ensure decisions were unified. This would have removed the division between the Party and the State.

[break]Hitler, by contrast, was mostly a non-interventionist dictator when it came to government administration. His occasional orders, when he gave them, were usually vague and given verbally, often through Lammers, the head of the Reich Chancellery, or, during the war years (for civilian issues), increasingly through Bormann.

After the early years of the regime, Hitler stopped chairing any formal committees. The Cabinet, which he disliked leading, gradually disappeared. He actively worked against efforts by Reich Interior Minister Frick to bring order and consistency to administration. He did a lot to maintain and strengthen the deep conflict between the Party and the State that existed at every level.
[break]Stalin seemed to deliberately shake up the government, which could lead to challenges from the bureaucracy.

But Hitler didn't seem to have a plan to destabilize the government. Instead, because of his leadership style that didn't rely on bureaucracy and his need to stay above political fights and unpopular policies, the government's rational ways of working gradually broke down. While the idea of "feudal anarchy" could describe both regimes, it fits the Hitler regime better.

From the start, personal loyalty was the main factor in power in Hitler's regime, completely overshadowing official roles and status. Personalities aside, Hitler's position as a leader seems to have been more secure in structure than Stalin's. If I've followed the debates correctly, there appears to have been some rational reason for Stalin's purges, even though the dictator's paranoia pushed them into fantasy.

As the supporter of one party line among several, one set of policies among many options, and one interpretation of the Marx-Lenin ideas among others, Stalin remained a leader who could be challenged from within. Kirov, it seems, had the potential to become a real rival leader in the early nineteen thirties, when many people were dissatisfied and unhappy with Stalin's rule.

At that time, Stalin's extreme sense of insecurity had some basis in reality. The purges that he started, and which often targeted people close to him, were mainly meant to prevent a bureaucratic challenge to his leadership. Hitler thought Stalin must be crazy to carry out the purges.

The only similar events in the Third Reich were the killing of the SA leaders during the "Night of the Long Knives" in nineteen thirty-four, and the brutal retaliation after the attempt on Hitler's life in nineteen forty-four. In the first case, Hitler agreed to the purge only late and unwillingly, after Himmler and Göring had already taken action, with support from the army leadership.

The second case is somewhat similar to the Stalinist method, although by then the Hitler regime was clearly near collapse. The harsh punishment of those involved in the assassination attempt was a last-ditch effort and mainly targeted real enemies, not a fundamental way of ruling. Until the middle of the war, Hitler's position was not as unstable as Stalin's leadership had been in the nineteen thirties.

Stalin could not trust even his closest supporters, but Hitler built his power on a principle of personal loyalty that he could always rely on during crises. He was unwilling to remove even people who were widely disliked and discredited, like Streicher, because in Hitler's view, Streicher had earned his support through loyalty and service in the movement's early years.
Hitler was visibly upset in the bunker when he heard about Himmler's betrayal - the "loyal Heinrich" finally turning against him.

[break]A serious challenge to Hitler, especially after Hindenburg died, could only come from within the armed forces (working together with a small, unhappy but not representative group among the conservative elites) or from a random attack by a lone assassin (like the one that nearly killed Hitler in nineteen thirty-nine).
Even in nineteen forty-four, the leaders of the failed coup knew they were alone and had no real support from the public for what they did.

It has to be accepted that for most of the time he was in power, Hitler was a very popular leader among both the ruling groups and the general public, even though he was outside the reach of the oppressed and powerless followers of the old working-class movements, parts of Catholicism, and a few individuals in the traditional elites.

[break]Within the Nazi Movement itself, his status was quite different from Stalin's position within the Communist Party. There are obvious similarities between the personality cults built around Stalin and Hitler. But while the Stalin cult was placed on top of the Marxist-Leninist ideology and the Communist Party, and both could survive without it, the "Hitler myth" was essential to the Nazi Movement.

In fact, it was the very foundation of the movement and almost impossible to separate from it or from the Nazi Weltanschauung. Since the mid-nineteen twenties, sticking to the official Nazi ideology meant following Hitler. Hitler supposedly told Otto Strasser in nineteen thirty, "For us the Idea is the Führer, and each Party member has only to obey the Führer."

Building up a "Führer party" pushed different or opposing views to the edges, then out of the party entirely. By the time the Nazi regime was set up and made strong, there was no position within Nazism that allowed a basic challenge to Hitler. His leadership, as the source of correct ideology and the perfect example of Nazism, was not questioned inside the movement.

Opposing Hitler on key issues was not possible, even among the top and most powerful people in the party. Using Hitler's name was the way to get ahead and succeed. Challenging the ideas tied to Hitler's leadership made it impossible to climb the ladder to status and power.

[break]Stalin's rule, for all its dynamic radicalism in the brutal collectivisation programme, the drive to industrialisation and the paranoid phase of the purges, was. Noakes and Pridham, Nazism, i. one hundred twelve to one hundred fourteen (based on an unpublished vivid, post-war account by Hinrich Lohse held in the Forschungsstelle für die Geschichte des Nationalsozialismus, Hamburg).

I am grateful to Jeremy Noakes for letting me see a photocopy of this document. This was not incompatible with setting priorities in a logical way and achieving goals that were limited and easy to understand, even though the methods used were extremely brutal and the cruelty involved was beyond belief.

People might still argue whether these methods were the best way to reach the goals, but trying to push industrialization at a very fast pace in a very underdeveloped economy and trying to create 'socialism in one country' cannot be seen as unreasonable or as having no limits. And even though the way led to a personalized dictatorship, there was no unavoidable "cumulative radicalization" in the Soviet Union.

Instead, by the mid-nineteen thirties there was even a "great retreat" from radicalism and a return to some forms of social conservativism before the war brought its own compromises with strict ideological correctness.

No matter how high the cost of personal control, and no matter how destructive Stalin was in purging the party and the military, the structures of the Soviet system were not completely destroyed. Stalin had come from the system. And the system was able to endure almost three decades of Stalin and outlast him. In other words, it was a system that could reproduce itself, even at the expense of a Stalin.

[break]It would be hard to say this about Nazism. The goal of national redemption through racial purification and a racial empire was a fantasy, a utopian idea. The cruelty and destruction that came from trying to achieve this goal were endless, just like the expansion and attacks on other peoples were limitless.

While Stalinism could settle down, as it did after Stalin died, into a static, even conservative, repressive system, something like that settling down into the kind of steady authoritarianism seen under Franco is hard to imagine with Nazism. With Nazism, the drive was constant, the push toward more radical action kept speeding up and couldn't be stopped unless the system itself was completely changed.

[break]I used the word "system" to describe Nazism. But while Soviet communism under Stalin, even with the dictator's violent disruptions, could still be recognized as a system of rule, the Hitler regime opposed any rational order of government and administration. Its main feature was a lack of system, disorder in administration and government, and the breakdown of clear patterns of governance, no matter how despotic.

[break]This was already clear in Germany before the war as government and administrative institutions and structures weakened, were worn down, or simply ignored, and disappeared. It was not just about the unresolved conflict between the Party and the State.
The growing number of "special authorities" and officials given specific tasks by the Führer and reporting directly to him showed the aggressive nature and improvised methods built into Nazi control.

The lack of clear planning for achievable medium-term goals, the absence of any place for group decision-making, the use of power in an arbitrary way based on the "leadership principle" at every level, the Darwinian idea of unrestricted struggle and competition until someone won,

and the simple belief in the "triumph of the will," no matter what challenges had to be faced - all these factors supported and influenced each other to create a chaotic system of competing and overlapping governing bodies. During the war, the breakdown of anything that looked like a state system happened very quickly.

In the occupied areas, the Nazi "new order" pushed out clear systems of control and replaced them with wild, uncoordinated power struggles among different groups. By the time Goebbels wrote in his diary in March nineteen forty-three about a "leadership crisis" - and in private called it a "leader crisis" - the system of government was beyond saving.

Hitler's leadership was central to the regime, but it did not work well with rational decision-making or a clear, unified administration that could achieve specific goals. The system's ability to destroy itself was obvious, and its collapse was certain. Hitler was essential to Nazism in a way that Stalin was not to Soviet Communism.

His position made it impossible to create any system for choosing a successor. No plan was ever made to handle Hitler's succession. The idea of a party senate, often talked about, never happened. Hitler refused any kind of institutional control. By nineteen forty-three, the removal of Mussolini by the Fascist Grand Council showed clearly that no party body could exist independently of the Leader in Germany.

Although Göring was named as the next in line, his chances of taking over became less likely as his influence clearly declined during the war. No other high-ranking Nazi leader was a real possibility to succeed Hitler. It is hard to imagine who could have taken over or how Hitler's personal rule could have been turned into a system. The regime, it must be said, could not continue on its own.
[break]The objection that, except for a lost war, there was nothing stopping this from happening, seems wrong.

The war was not a side issue for Nazism. It was central to it. The war had to happen and could not be delayed until a better time. And by the end of nineteen forty-one, even though the war continued for another three and a half years, the attempt to become a 'world power' was already lost in reality. Because of this, the energy driving the regime and its self-destructive nature can be seen as inseparable.
[break]This brings me back to the questions I asked at the start of this paper.

If my understanding of recent discussions about Stalinism is not completely wrong, and if the differences I have pointed out between the Hitler regime and Stalin's have some truth, then it is fair to say that, even though there may be some surface similarities, the nature of the dictatorship - meaning Stalin's and Hitler's roles as leaders in their respective regimes - was fundamentally different.

But it would be too narrow to explain these differences only by the personalities of the dictators. Instead, I think these differences should be seen as a result of the different motivations of their followers, the nature of the ideas driving each regime, and the kind of political movement that supported each one.

To put it plainly, the Nazi movement was a typical example of a "charismatic" leadership movement, while the Soviet Communist Party was not. And this has an effect on how each system of rule was able to continue and reproduce itself. Max Weber described the main features of "charismatic authority" clearly, so there's no need to go into more detail here.
It involves a leader who is seen as having a heroic "mission" and is believed to be great by their followers.

This kind of authority often appears during crises as a quick solution. It is naturally unstable because it faces two constant threats: the loss of "charisma" when the leader fails to meet expectations, and the transformation into a "system" that can continue on its own by removing, subordinating, or absorbing the original "charismatic" qualities.

In its pure form, the personal control of "charismatic authority" contradicts and negates the impersonal, role-based use of power that is central to the bureaucratic, legally rational authority of the "ideal type" modern state. In fact, it cannot become a system without losing its unique "charismatic" quality.
Max Weber did imagine ways for "charisma" to be part of an institution, but these involve compromises with the pure form. The idea of "charismatic authority" clearly fits Hitler.

But it's less clear for Stalin. In Stalin's case, the "mission" could be seen as belonging to the Communist Party, which carries the Marxist-Leninist doctrine. For a time, Stalin took over this "mission" and tried to make it all about himself through his personality cult. But this cult came later and was added on artificially to Stalin's real role.

This is very different from Hitler's personality cult, which was tied to the "mission" from the start. By the mid-1920s at the latest, this "mission" was not a separate doctrine but was instead linked to the leader himself. Weber's idea of "charismatic authority" is a general concept. It doesn't describe the actual content of any specific example of charismatic authority.

What makes a charismatic claim meaningful depends on how the leader's demands fit the specific situation and political culture in which they appear. The core of Hitler's charismatic claim was his "mission" to bring about "national rebirth" through racial purity and a racial empire.

But in practice, this claim was vague, flexible, and shapeless enough to fit easily with more traditional forms of nationalism and imperialism, which had a long history dating back to the Kaiserreich.

The trauma of war, defeat, and "national disgrace," followed by the extreme conditions of a state system in the final stages of collapse and a nation deeply divided internally, created the opportunity for this charismatic claim to gain widespread support. It extended far beyond the original group of followers and became the foundation for a completely new kind of state.

[break]In a modern state, replacing a well-functioning bureaucracy with personal control is clearly impossible. Even when both 'legal-rational' and 'charismatic' forms of legitimacy exist together, they create tension and conflict, possibly leading to serious dysfunction.
What happened in the Third Reich was not the replacement of bureaucratic control by 'charismatic authority,' but the placing of charismatic authority on top of the bureaucracy.

When constitutional law was now seen as nothing more than 'the legal expression of the historic will of the Führer' - believed to come from his 'remarkable accomplishments' - and when Germany's top constitutional lawyer could say that 'state power' had been replaced by unchecked 'Führer power,' the result was the weakening of the impersonal legal foundation that modern 'legal-rational' state systems depend on.

This led to the breakdown of organized government and established administrative structures, replaced by unrestrained personal control. The main source of legitimacy for this control was the 'charismatic claim,' the 'vision' of national renewal. The unstoppable breakdown into 'systemlessness' was, therefore, not mainly a matter of 'will'.

Certainly, Hitler was allergic to any hint of practical or theoretical limits on his power. But there was no systematic 'divide and rule' policy, no ongoing effort to create the administrative chaos of the Third Reich.

It was, indeed, partly a reflection of Hitler's personality and his leadership style: as already mentioned, he was extremely unbureaucratic, stayed away from the daily work of government, and had no interest in complicated details. But this non-bureaucratic style was itself more than just a personal quirk or oddity.

It was an unavoidable result of the deification of the leadership role itself and the resulting need to maintain prestige that matched the created image. His instinctive Darwinism made him unwilling and unable to take sides in a dispute until a winner emerged. But the need to protect his image of being always right also made him largely unable to do so.

[break]It was not just the breaking down of rational government structures and the rise of chaotic, polycratic agencies that was important. What mattered was that this process went along with and helped push forward a gradual realization of ideological goals. These goals were closely tied to the "mission" of the "charismatic" Leader.

As the "idea" of Nazism, embodied in the person of the Führer, was turned from a utopian "vision" into practical reality between nineteen thirty-eight and nineteen forty-two, there was a close, mutually supporting relationship between the disorder in the structure of the Nazi state and the hardening of policy.

[break]The key development was clearly the growing independence of the Führer's authority, reaching a point by 1938 at the latest where it was not limited in practice or theory by any government institutions or other power structures. After the Blomberg-Fritsch affair in February nineteen thirty-eight, it was hard to see where the structures or individuals capable of stopping Hitler still existed.

By this time, pressures partly caused by the dictator's own actions, but more so by diplomatic and economic events beyond his control, encouraged and even shaped the high-risk approach that was already Hitler's natural tendency. At the same time, along with the expansion into Austria and the Sudetenland in nineteen thirty-eight, race policy also moved forward more quickly.

The Reichskristallnacht attack in November, started by Goebbels not Hitler - although done with Hitler's clear approval - was the peak of the more extreme actions of the past year or so. It ended by putting the coordination of the 'Jewish Question' under Heydrich's control. Hitler's territorial expansion and his plan to remove the Jews were the two main parts of his Weltanschauung.

By nineteen thirty-eight, these ideas were clearly visible in the foreground. The move from a utopian vision to actual policy choices was beginning to take form. It would be wrong to look only, or even mainly, at Hitler's own actions as the reason the regime kept becoming more extreme. Hitler was the central figure of the whole "system," the only person connecting its different parts.

But for the most part, he wasn't directly needed to push the radicalization forward. What seems most important, then, is how "charismatic authority" actually worked to break down any system of "rational" government that might have acted as a limit. This allowed the radicalization to happen mostly through the actions of others, without clear direction from Hitler.
[break]Hitler's 'charismatic' Führer position had three main functions in the Third Reich: bringing people together, driving action, and making things possible.

[break]As unifier, the "idea" included in the almost godlike Führer figure was vague enough but also strong enough to serve as a link not only for groups within the Nazi Movement that would otherwise fight each other but also, until it was too late to pull away from the dangerous path, for non-Nazi national-conservative leaders in the army, economy, and government.

It also provided the main support from the public for the regime. This support gave Hitler repeated approval from the people for his actions. It also gave a common base for the main agreement in Nazi policy to form around. As activator, the "vision" embodied by Hitler acted as a motivator for action across the different parts of the Nazi Movement.

In these parts, people with unused energy and unmet social expectations could take action in Hitler's name to achieve the goals of the Leader and the Party. Outside the movement, this vision also encouraged action in the government bureaucracy, industry, and the armed forces. It also encouraged action among professionals like teachers, doctors, or lawyers.

For these groups, the idea of "national redemption" could offer a way to push forward long-held ambitions that had been blocked or harmed by the Weimar "system." In all these ways, the utopian "vision" connected with the Führer - vague and mostly impossible to define - gave "guidelines for action."

These guidelines took on real meaning and specific content through the active efforts of many different parts of the regime, often competing with each other. The most important, most energetic, and most closely tied to Hitler's ideological goals was, of course, the SS. In the SS, the "idea" or "vision" allowed for constant new initiatives in an ongoing cycle of discrimination, repression, and persecution.

[break]Perhaps most important of all, as enabler Hitler's authority gave quiet support and approval to those whose actions, however cruel, however extreme, fit within the general and vague idea of helping the Führer's goals.

Creating a 'national community', getting ready for the fight with Bolshevism, cleaning the Reich of its political and biological or racial enemies, and driving Jews out of Germany, gave people free permission to take actions that, unless they were badly timed or harmful, were more or less sure to get approval from the top.

The drop in civilized behavior that started in the spring of nineteen thirty-three, and the growing extreme of discrimination and persecution that followed, were not only not stopped but always found support from the highest authority in the country. A key part of this "progress into barbarism" was that in nineteen thirty-three, the obstacles to government-approved acts of extreme cruelty were removed very quickly.

[break]for November tenth, nineteen thirty-eight is available in Ralf Georg Reuth, ed., Joseph Goebbels. Diaries (Munich: Piper, 1992), iii. one thousand two hundred eighty-one to one thousand two hundred eighty-two. What had once seemed impossible suddenly became possible.

New opportunities quickly appeared, and they were quickly taken. The Sterilisation Law of July nineteen thirty-three is an early example of this removal of barriers. Ideas that eugenicists had long supported in biological-social engineering suddenly found a setting where they could be put into action without the limits that were still assumed in earlier proposals.

These earlier proposals, though already inhumane, were limited to voluntary sterilisation. They had been put forward by the German Doctors' Association just weeks before Hitler took power. By nineteen thirty-nine the loss of civilised values had gone far enough to allow for the possibility of killing as 'useless life' those considered harmful to the spread of 'healthy comrades of the people'.

And, showing how far the breakdown of the government system had gone, when written permission was needed, it came not from a government law or decree (which Hitler specifically refused) but from a few lines typed on Hitler's private letterhead.
Those few lines were enough to decide the fate of over seventy thousand mentally ill and physically disabled people in Germany by mid-nineteen forty-one in the so-called 'euthanasia action'.

[break]After nineteen thirty-nine, in the parts of Poland taken over by Germany and added to the Reich, Hitler's call for brutal methods in a "racial struggle" that ignored legal limits led to no more limits on cruelty toward the Polish people and the Jewish minority there.

Hitler didn't need to push for the increasing brutality to go faster. He could leave it to the local rulers. As usual, he said he expected nothing more from his Gauleiter in the East than that after ten years they could say their areas were completely German.

This alone was enough to start a contest in brutality - even though this supposedly went against what Hitler wanted - between the rival regional leaders Albert Forster in West Prussia and Arthur Greiser in the Warthegau to be the first to tell the Führer that the "racial struggle" was won and complete Germanization had been achieved.

[break]The license that Hitler, as an "enabler," gave to certain party leaders in the East can be clearly shown by the "initiative" taken by Greiser in May nineteen forty-two, when he suggested the killing of thirty five thousand Poles who had incurable tuberculosis.

In the end, Greiser's suggestion ran into problems. Some people objected, saying it would be hard to keep the plan secret - this was because of the problems caused by the earlier "euthanasia program" in Germany itself. They also said the plan would probably cause unrest among the Polish people and give foreign propaganda an opportunity. It was thought necessary to get Hitler's approval before the "action" could proceed.

Greiser responded by saying, "I myself do not believe that the Führer needs to be asked again in this matter, especially since at our last discussion regarding the Jews he told me that I could proceed with these according to my own judgment."

This judgment had already been to recommend to Himmler the "special treatment" (that is, killing) of one hundred thousand Jews in the Warthegau - the start of the "final solution" there. Greiser saw himself as the direct agent and tool of the Führer in the campaign to build his "model Gau." He met any obstacles by saying his authority to Germanize the Warthegau came from special powers given to him personally by the Führer.

[break]The connection between the Führer, who acted as a 'symbol' for actionism, and the spread of extreme ideas, along with the push 'from below' by many groups, both non-Nazi and Nazi, to turn the 'vision' or parts of it into real policies is shown well in the words of a typical Nazi official's speech in nineteen thirty-four.

[break]Everyone who has the chance to see it knows that the Führer can hardly tell everyone from the top down everything he wants to achieve sooner or later. On the contrary, so far, people in positions in the new Germany have done their best when they have, as it were, worked toward the Führer. Often and in many areas, it has been the case - in the past as well - that individuals simply waited for orders and instructions.
Unfortunately, this will also be true in the future. But in reality, it is everyone's duty to try to work toward the Führer in the way he would want. Anyone who makes mistakes will soon notice it.

But anyone who truly works toward the Führer in his way and toward his goal will certainly, both now and in the future, one day receive the finest reward in the form of sudden legal confirmation of their work.

[break]These comments hint at the way 'charismatic authority' worked in the Third Reich - looking ahead to Hitler's expected wishes and intentions as guidelines for action. For a longer discussion, see my article "Improvised Genocide?

The Emergence of the 'Final Solution' in the 'Warthegau'," Transactions of the Royal Historical Society, sixth Series, Volume two (1992), pages fifty-one to seventy-eight, specifically pages seventy-one to seventy-three. "Action" in the certainty of approval and confirmation for actions that matched those wishes and intentions.
[break]"Working towards the Führer" can be understood in a straightforward way when referring to party officials, as it was used in the passage quoted.

For the SS, the group responsible for carrying out the "Führer's will," the idea of "working towards the Führer" gave them endless opportunities to take brutal actions. These actions also brought more power, influence, status, and wealth to the organization.

The career of Adolf Eichmann, who started in a low-level position in a major policy area and eventually became in charge of the "Final Solution," is a clear example of this. But the idea of "working towards the Führer" can also be understood in a more indirect way. In this case, people might not be motivated by ideology at all. Still, their actions help make it possible to carry out Hitler's goals.

For example, someone trying to get ahead in the party or government by gaining money and status, a small business owner trying to ruin a competitor by falsely accusing them of not being "Aryan," or a regular citizen trying to get revenge by reporting a neighbor to the Gestapo - these people are all, in a way, "working towards the Führer."

Doctors who quickly suggest patients in mental hospitals for the "euthanasia program," believing it will create a more "eugenically healthy" population; lawyers and judges who eagerly help remove legal protections to get rid of "criminals" and other unwanted people;

business leaders who want to profit from war preparations and, once war starts, by seizing resources and using foreign slave labor; ambitious technocrats and scientists who want to gain power and influence by joining the push for technological progress; military leaders not in the Nazi party who want to build a strong army and bring back German dominance in central Europe;

and traditional conservatives who dislike the Nazis but fear the Bolsheviks even more - each of these groups, in their own way, supports the system through their actions. This support, even if indirect, leads to the system becoming more extreme and to policies that align more closely with the ideas Hitler represents. Hitler repeatedly set a brutal tone.

He did this in hate-filled public speeches that encouraged discrimination against Jews and other "enemies of the state." He also did it in private addresses to Nazi officials and military leaders. In those meetings, he gave brutal guidelines for the occupation of Poland and for "Operation Barbarossa."

There was never a shortage of willing helpers. These helpers were not just party activists. They were ready to "work towards the Führer" to carry out Hitler's orders. Once the war - which was central to Nazism and Hitler's "vision" - began, the barbarism inspired by that "vision" reached unimaginable depths. There was no chance, and could never have been a chance, for the "New Order" to become a real system of government.

Competing fiefdoms, not a structured government, were the grim reality of Nazi rule in the occupied territories. The greed and destruction that had been present in Germany from the start now became much worse. The conquered peoples, not the Germans themselves, were now the main victims.

[break]Using the metaphor of "working towards the Führer," I have tried to show that the "vision" behind Hitler's leadership claim helped channel many different social motivations, sometimes conflicting, into supporting - on purpose or by accident - Nazi goals that were closely tied to Hitler's own extreme ideas.

In this view, the idea of "charismatic authority" is helpful for describing the connections that different social and political groups formed with Hitler. This allowed the kind of personal power he represented to escape all institutional limits and to justify the destructive drive behind the Nazi push for control over Europe through war.

[break]The model of 'charismatic authority', which I have suggested is applicable to the Hitlerian but not to the Stalinist dictatorship, not only helps to describe the appeal of a quasi-messianic, personalized form of rule that embodies national unity and rebirth in the context of the collapse of the democratic system of Weimar.

It also, given the irreconcilable tension between 'charismatic authority' and bureaucratic rule in the Third Reich, offers insights into the inevitable erosion of anything resembling a system of domination capable of reproducing itself.

Within this 'Behemoth' of governmental disorder, 'working towards the Führer' amounted to a selective push for the radicalisation and implementation of those ideological lines most closely associated with Hitler's known broad aims, which could gradually take shape as policy objectives rather than distant goals.

[break]Most importantly, the 'charismatic' model matches a kind of control that could never become normal or routine, never accept its successes and settle into a conservative authoritarian form, but instead had to keep up the energy and constantly push for new achievements in the effort to reach its unrealistic goal. The longer the Hitler regime lasted, the more grandiose its goals became, and the more destructive it was.

But the longer the regime continued, the less it looked like a government system that could keep going on its own. This type of "charismatic authority" was unstable because the "charismatic claim" was based on a utopian goal of national redemption through racial purity, war, and conquest. This instability meant not only that it was destructive but also that it destroyed itself.
In this way, Hitler's own tendency toward suicide could be seen as showing the built-in inability of his form of authoritarian rule to last or continue.
